sections.h2: How a Delaware sheriff sale works
sections.html:
A sheriff sale is a public auction of real estate run by the county sheriff to satisfy a court judgment, usually a mortgage foreclosure or unpaid taxes. The highest bidder wins, and the Superior Court then confirms the sale before any deed is delivered.

Delaware has three counties, and each sheriff runs sales a little differently. You'll run into mortgage foreclosure sales, tax sales (also called monition sales) and, in some counties, goods and chattels sales involving personal property.

  • Foreclosure sales: the plaintiff's attorney gives the opening bid, then bidders raise it out loud.
  • Tax or monition sales: the county or town sells a property for unpaid taxes or fees, and the owner may redeem afterward.
  • Confirmation: the court reviews the sale before the sheriff signs a deed.

For an owner facing a sale date, the real questions are how much time is left and what can be done before the auction.

sections.h2: Sale dates, places and payment deadlines
sections.html:
Kent County holds mortgage foreclosure sales usually on the first Thursday of the month. Sussex County holds them on the third Tuesday of each month at 9:30 a.m. Sales happen at government buildings, never at the property.

Kent County advertises its sales in the Dover Post and the Delaware State News two weeks ahead, and its tax sales come around about every three months.

The sheriff has to advertise the sale, and the plaintiff has to send notice to interested parties. Under 10 Del. C. section 4973, notice of a real estate sale goes up at least 10 days before the sale in 10 public places in the county, including the hundred where the property lies and each adjoining hundred, and runs for two weeks in two newspapers.

Superior Court Civil Rule 69(g) adds a mailing duty. At least seven days before the sale, the plaintiff or its counsel sends notice by certified mail, return receipt requested, to lienholders, tenants, record owners and other holders of recorded interests. The notice is also posted on a common entrance or area of the building. No sheriff's sale goes forward until proof of mailing and posting has been filed.

A July 2026 Superior Court order shows why notice matters. In New Castle County v. Coleman, the court set aside a June 9, 2026 sale of a Newark property and denied confirmation because the first mortgage holder never got actual notice that a stay had been lifted. The sale price was roughly half of that holder's security interest.

sections.h2: Payment and default rules for the winning bidder
sections.html:
The winner pays a deposit on sale day and the balance about a month later. A bidder who fails to pay forfeits the deposit, and the property is sold again.

  • Deposit: $4,000 in Kent County, by cashier's check, certified check or money order payable to the sheriff, applied toward the 20 percent down payment.
  • Foreclosure down payment: Kent wants the rest of the 20 percent by 2:00 p.m. on sale day, with the 80 percent balance due about 30 days later on the third Monday of the following month. Sussex wants 20 percent by 3 p.m. and the balance on the third Monday of the following month.
  • Forfeiture: in Kent, a buyer who misses the 2:00 p.m. payment loses the deposit and may be barred from future sales. In Sussex, failing to pay the balance forfeits the sale and the non-refundable 20 percent.
  • As-is: Sussex properties sell as-is and sight unseen, bidders may not trespass, and the winner is responsible for any liens.

Neither county guarantees clear title. Both tell bidders to search the Recorder of Deeds and the Prothonotary's Office first.

The sale is taxed too. Under 30 Del. C. section 5404, realty transfer tax is paid first out of the proceeds of a judicial sale, except where the buyer files an affidavit that the transfer to a defaulted lender is exempt.

Under Superior Court Civil Rule 69(d), the sheriff's return is due on the third Monday of the month after the sale. Objections must be filed by the first Thursday after the return date. With no objection, the sale is confirmed automatically the following Friday.

Sussex County describes the same rhythm: sales are confirmed on the first Friday after the third Monday of the following month. In Kent County, the buyer's attorney prepares the deed after confirmation and the sheriff signs it.

After confirmation, 10 Del. C. section 4976 requires the sheriff to deliver a good and sufficient deed. Section 4985 discharges the real estate from liens against the defendant, except prior mortgages, to the extent the sale proceeds apply. Under section 4978, the purchaser is entitled to rent from the day of sale.

Ownership changes only when a proper deed is recorded. Our guide to recording a Delaware deed covers the fees and affidavits.

sections.h2: Money left over after the sale
sections.html:
Sometimes, yes. If a sale brings in more than the debt, the court may hold the excess. Delaware's Superior Court runs Project Rightful Owner, a page listing former owners, sold property addresses, court-held amounts, sale dates and case numbers for New Castle, Kent and Sussex counties.

Under 10 Del. C. section 4986, proceeds that can't be paid because the entitled persons are absent, unknown or incompetent go to the court that issued the process. Paying into court discharges the selling officer from liability for that money.

The Project Rightful Owner pages point claimants to petition requirements and attorney listings. If you lost a house at a sheriff sale in the past, search the list by surname.

sections.h2: What to do before your house goes to sale
sections.html:
You can sell the house before the sale date, and a sale before the auction lets you keep any equity. Kent County's procedures give tax sales a redemption period of about 90 days, with the buyer getting the bid back plus 15 percent if the owner redeems. Foreclosure sales carry no redemption period.

In Sussex County, monition property can't be possessed until 60 days after confirmation, and sheriff sale property comes with no automatic eviction of occupants. An auction buyer has to plan for that.

Steps worth taking:

  • Get the exact sale date and case number from the sheriff and the Prothonotary.
  • Ask the plaintiff's attorney for a payoff figure.
  • Weigh whether a buyer who closes quickly beats the auction result.
  • Ask about loss-mitigation and mediation steps, which apply to owner-occupied homes.

A cash buyer can often close faster than an auction timeline allows, but the sale still has to pay off the liens of record. Cash Home Buyers can't promise a price and will go over the numbers with you.

faqs.q: What is a sheriff sale in Delaware?
faqs.a: It's a public auction of real estate run by the county sheriff under a court order, usually after a mortgage foreclosure or for unpaid taxes. The Superior Court must confirm the sale before a deed is delivered.

faqs.q: Is there a redemption period after a Delaware foreclosure sale?
faqs.a: Kent County says foreclosure sales have none. Tax sales do: the owner has 60 days after the court approves the sale to redeem by paying the buyer the price plus 15 percent and costs.

faqs.q: How much do I need to bid at a Delaware sheriff sale?
faqs.a: Kent and Sussex counties both require a $4,000 deposit to bid. On a foreclosure the winner then pays 20 percent of the bid in total on sale day and the balance by the third Monday of the following month.

faqs.q: Do sheriff sale buyers get the keys right away?
faqs.a: No. Occupants aren't automatically evicted in Sussex County, and buyers may not enter before confirmation. Ownership changes when a proper deed is recorded.

faqs.q: Can a sheriff sale be stopped or postponed?
faqs.a: In Sussex County a sale can be stayed until 9:30 a.m. on sale day. Courts can also set a sale aside for irregularities, as in New Castle County v. Coleman in 2026, so watch for notice of any change.
